issues.legal_issue: An objection to an arbitral award is not time-barred when the prescribed notice that the award has been filed in court was not served.
material_facts: A party sued to have the award made a rule of court.
The opposing party challenged the award in its written statement.
There was no proof that the opposing party had been served with notice that the award had been filed in court.
issues.conclusion: The objection to the award could not be rejected as time-barred.
issues.legal_principle: Article 158 of the Limitation Act, 1908, allows 30 days to apply to set aside an award or have it remitted, running from service of notice of the filing of the award. Without proof of service of that notice, the time period does not bar the objection.

predicates.award_objection_proceeding: A party to an arbitration challenges the award in a court proceeding to have it set aside or remitted.
predicates.notice_of_award_filing_not_served: The party challenging the award was not served with notice that the award had been filed in court.
predicates.award_objection_is_timely: The objection to the award is not barred by the applicable time limit.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an arbitral award in court and was not served with notice of its filing, the objection is timely.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitrator's reliance on personal knowledge, without informing the parties of that knowledge and giving them an opportunity to respond, vitiates the award when the reference does not specifically authorize that method of decision.
material_facts: The arbitrators decided the dispute primarily on the basis of their personal knowledge.
The agreement permitted the arbitrators to decide in whatever manner they thought fit but did not specifically authorize reliance on personal knowledge.
The parties were not informed of the nature of the arbitrators' personal knowledge or given an opportunity to correct any misconception or wrong assumption.
issues.conclusion: The arbitrators committed legal misconduct, and the award was vitiated.
issues.legal_principle: Arbitration proceedings are quasi-judicial and must comply with natural justice. A general term allowing arbitrators to decide in whatever manner they think fit does not authorize them to decide on personal knowledge. Parties may include terms in a reference unless prohibited by law, and the ordinary implied requirement that arbitrators decide according to law may be displaced only by specific provision. Arbitrators must disclose the nature of personal knowledge relied on and allow the parties an opportunity to respond. The Court referred to Chandris v. Isbrandtsen Moller Co. Inc., [1951] K.B. 240, on the ordinary implied term that arbitrators decide according to the ordinary law.

predicates.arbitration_proceeding: The dispute was referred to arbitrators for a decision.
predicates.arbitrators_relied_on_personal_knowledge: The arbitrators based their decision on knowledge they personally possessed about the dispute.
predicates.parties_not_informed_and_given_opportuni: The arbitrators did not disclose the nature of that personal knowledge to the parties and give them an opportunity to respond to it.
predicates.award_is_vitiated: The award is invalid because the arbitrators committed legal misconduct.

issues.definition: An award is vitiated when arbitrators deciding a referred dispute rely on their personal knowledge without informing the parties of it and giving them an opportunity to respond.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may decline to interfere under its special-leave jurisdiction when the High Court's decision is eminently just, even if the High Court may have exceeded its revisional powers.
material_facts: The appeal was brought by special leave against a High Court decision made in revision.
The Supreme Court considered the High Court's decision eminently just.
The Supreme Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the High Court could correct the lower appellate court's interpretation in revision.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary power, and the Court may decline to interfere where the decision under appeal is eminently just, even assuming that the lower court may have lacked the revisional power in question.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: A party brings an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave against a High Court decision.
predicates.high_court_decision_is_eminently_just: The Supreme Court considers the High Court's decision eminently just.
predicates.special_leave_interference_is_declined: The Supreme Court declines to interfere with the High Court's decision.

issues.definition: In an appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court may decline to interfere when it considers the High Court's decision eminently just.
